explain: Thousands of guessed paths in a short time, mostly missing, are the fingerprint of a content discovery scanner looking for admin panels, backups and exposed repositories. The rare 200 among them is the line to investigate first.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A 4-node server's distance table shows 10 on the diagonal and 20 everywhere else. What is the safest reading?
options: Every remote access costs exactly twice a local one
Remote access is roughly twice as costly as local, but firmware tables can be inaccurate, so measure
The machine is actually UMA because all remote entries are equal
explain: SLIT values are relative estimates normalized to 10 for local access. Drepper shows a real table that reported 20 for every pair even though some pairs had to be two hops apart. Use the table as a hint and benchmark when placement matters.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: A database pins each worker to one node and places every buffer with explicit mbind policies. Profiling shows time spent in page faults on pages that never move. What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable MPOL_INTERLEAVE on all buffers
Use smaller pages so faults are cheaper
Disable automatic NUMA balancing for this workload
explain: These are NUMA hinting faults from automatic balancing sampling pages that are already correctly placed. The kernel docs recommend disabling balancing when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
question: A service writes 300 TB per year to a 1 TB drive rated for 10,000 P/E cycles. The drive's FDP statistics show media bytes written are 5x host bytes. Roughly how long until rated wear-out?
options: About 6.7 years
About 33 years
About 1.3 years
Never, wear leveling prevents it
explain: Lifetime host writes = 1 TB x 10,000 / 5 = 2,000 TB. At 300 TB per year that is 2000/300, about 6.7 years. Halving A to 2.5 would double it.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
question: Why does DETR not need NMS at test time?
options: Its object queries are fixed to non-overlapping image regions
It applies NMS inside the transformer decoder
One-to-one Hungarian matching during training gives each object only one positive prediction, so other slots learn to predict 'no object'
It only predicts one object per image
explain: Object queries are learned embeddings, not fixed regions. Because the matching assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one slot, a second slot covering the same object is trained toward the no-object class. The DETR paper reports that adding NMS helps early decoder layers but slightly hurts AP at the last layer.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Batching writes: the cost versus latency dial
question: To cut latency further, an engineer changes the Agent to acknowledge a Produce request as soon as it lands in the in-memory buffer. What does this break?
options: Ordering within a partition
Nothing, since S3 is durable
Compaction, because files get smaller
Durability: if the Agent crashes before the PUT, acknowledged records are lost
explain: The buffer is memory in a stateless process. WarpStream never acknowledges a write until it is in object storage and committed to the metadata store, which is what lets it lose every Agent without losing acknowledged data. Acking from memory turns a crash into data loss.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
question: Checkout p99 reads 1.3 s and the orders database p99 reads 0.9 s, both rising in the same minute. What do the metrics alone establish?
options: That checkout requests are waiting on the database
That the database is the root cause, since it is the deepest component
That the two are correlated in time, but not that any single checkout request waited on the database
Nothing, because percentiles from different services are never comparable
explain: Metrics are per-component aggregates with no request identity, so simultaneity is a hypothesis, not a causal link. The slow checkout requests and the slow queries may even be disjoint sets. A trace carries parent and child spans and settles it for one request.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
question: Why does DBNet replace the hard threshold with a sigmoid of k(P - T)?
options: It makes inference faster than a comparison
It lets gradients flow so the network can learn a per-pixel threshold map
It removes the need for the probability map
It guarantees that adjacent words never merge
explain: A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere, so a threshold inside it cannot be learned. The steep sigmoid approximates the step but stays differentiable. At inference the paper actually drops this path and uses a constant threshold on P.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
question: Which bug is usually the most severe for a multi-user Linux server?
options: A crash in a user's text editor
A memory bug in a kernel system call that any process can make
A memory bug in a setuid program that only root can run
A typo in a log message
explain: A kernel bug reachable from any process can bypass every permission check, for every user and every container on the host. A setuid program that only root can run gives an attacker nothing new.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: AppArmor: path-based profiles that confine one program
question: What is the key design difference between AppArmor and SELinux?
options: AppArmor confines users, SELinux confines programs
AppArmor only works on Windows
AppArmor rules name paths a program uses; SELinux rules name types stored in labels on subjects and objects
SELinux is discretionary and AppArmor is mandatory
explain: Both are mandatory and both confine programs. AppArmor writes rules in terms of paths, which makes profiles readable; SELinux writes them in terms of types, so a file's label travels with it.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Namespaces and cgroups: the building blocks of containers
question: A process is root inside a user namespace (mapped to UID 1000 outside). It tries to set the system's calendar clock. What happens?
options: It changes the clock only for the container
It succeeds, because it has all capabilities in its namespace
It succeeds only inside a time namespace
It fails, because capabilities in a user namespace apply only to resources governed by that namespace, and the system clock is not one
explain: user_namespaces(7) uses this very example: changing the system time is governed by CAP_SYS_TIME in the initial namespace. Time namespaces offset only the boot and monotonic clocks.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs
question: An attacker has root on a server with kernel lockdown enabled and module signature enforcement on. What stops them loading a rootkit module they compiled?
options: Secure boot scans the disk at runtime
The rootkit must be in /lib/modules
The kernel refuses modules that are not validly signed with a trusted key, even for root
Nothing: root can do anything
explain: With enforcement, the kernel itself checks the signature at load time. Root controls the filesystem but does not hold the signing key, so the module is refused.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: What OSINT is, and what it is for
question: Under the Berkeley Protocol, which of these is closed-source information?
options: A company's published annual report
A satellite image anyone can buy from a commercial provider
Details an investigator learns by messaging an employee on a social network
A public video on a video-sharing site
explain: The Protocol treats information acquired "through communication with" internet users as closed source. Buying satellite imagery is fine: open source includes what the public can purchase.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
question: A `site:northwind.example filetype:pdf` search returns nothing. What can you conclude?
options: Northwind has no PDF files on any server
Google has not shown any indexed PDFs for that query; others may exist or be unindexed
Northwind blocks Google entirely
The query syntax was wrong
explain: Google documents that site: results are not always exhaustive. An empty result is evidence about the index, not about the server.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes
question: Why can a SHA-256 hash not find a resized repost of a photo, while dHash can?
options: SHA-256 is too slow for images
dHash uses a secret key
SHA-256 changes completely when any byte changes; dHash compares brightness patterns that resizing keeps
SHA-256 only works on text
explain: Cryptographic hashes are designed so any change gives an unrelated hash. dHash records which neighbour is brighter, a pattern that survives resizing and uniform brightness changes.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Archiving: capturing evidence that will still be trusted later
question: What does a matching SHA-256 hash, recomputed months later, prove?
options: That the web page was truthful
That the page never changed online
That the stored file is unchanged since its hash was recorded
Who wrote the page
explain: A hash proves integrity of the stored copy from the moment it was hashed. Truth, authorship and the live page's history need other evidence.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
question: A colleague says: "Ninja must re-scan all #include lines before every build, so a no-op build (one where nothing changed) of 10,000 files is slow." What does Ninja actually do?
options: It runs the preprocessor on every file to find includes
It ignores headers and only tracks .cpp timestamps
It reuses header lists the compiler reported in earlier builds (depfiles), stored in its own database
It asks CMake to recompute header dependencies on every run
explain: With deps = gcc, Ninja reads each depfile right after the compile and saves a compact form in an internal database, so a no-op build only has to stat files (ask the operating system for each file's modification time, without reading it), not preprocess them.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
question: Your branch passes all tests locally. CI on your PR fails in a test file you never touched. Since you branched, `main` gained 20 commits. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: The CI runner is broken and you should ask a maintainer to rerun it
CI tests the merge of your branch into the current `main`, and your change interacts badly with something that landed since you branched
GitHub Actions only runs tests in files changed by the PR, so it must be a caching bug
Your local Python is newer, so CI should be ignored
explain: For `pull_request` events GitHub tests the merge commit `refs/pull/N/merge`. Rebase or merge the latest `main` locally and rerun the tests to reproduce. Blaming the runner first is how real failures get dismissed; and Actions runs whatever the workflow says, not only changed files.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
question: A test passes alone, passes in file order, but fails about one run in five under `pytest -n 4` (pytest-xdist). Locally with `-p randomly` it also fails for some seeds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The test is too slow and xdist times it out
It depends on state another test sets up or leaves behind, so it breaks when the order or the worker process changes
xdist uses threads, which makes Python tests nondeterministic
Exit code 5 from xdist workers
explain: Failing under reordering and under parallel workers is the signature of order or state dependence. The pytest docs note that xdist spawns processes, not threads, and that tests relying on data from a previous test break when that test is on a different worker.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
question: A repository has no branch protection or rulesets. A maintainer submits Request changes on your PR. Can someone with merge rights still merge it?
options: No, Request changes always blocks merging until the reviewer approves
Yes, without a rule requiring reviews, Request changes is informational
No, GitHub requires at least two approvals by default
Only after the reviewer dismisses their own review
explain: GitHub's docs say Request changes is purely informational unless a ruleset or classic branch protection rule requires pull request reviews. The social signal still matters: merging over an unresolved request is a team decision, not a tool one.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
question: Under Contributor Covenant 2.1, a contributor gets a Warning with a 30-day no-contact period. A week later they message the person who reported them on social media to explain themselves. What follows?
options: Nothing: social media is outside the project's spaces
It is allowed because the contributor is apologising
It breaks the Warning's terms, which cover external channels like social media, and can lead to a temporary or permanent ban
The Warning is cancelled and replaced by a Correction
explain: A Warning forbids interaction with the people involved for a set period, including unsolicited contact and external channels like social media. The text says violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
question: Your branch has commits P (parser), T (tests), then a `fixup! parser` commit F. After `git rebase -i --autosquash upstream/main`, what does the todo list contain?
options: pick P, pick T, fixup F
pick P, pick T, squash F
fixup F, pick P, pick T
pick P, fixup F, pick T
explain: Autosquash moves each `fixup!` commit directly after the commit whose title it names and turns its `pick` into `fixup`. So F lands between P and T. `squash` is used only for `squash!` commits, and a fixup never runs before its target.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
question: A bank modifies a GPL-3.0 command-line tool and runs it on internal servers only. An employee asks for the modified source to publish on GitHub. What does the license require?
options: The bank must publish the source within a reasonable time
Nothing: in-house use is not conveying, so no source obligation arises
The bank must give the source to that employee only
The bank must switch to the AGPL
explain: Using a program inside one organization is not conveying, and the GPL FAQ confirms an organization can use a modified version internally without releasing it. Obligations start only when copies go to others.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
question: Which PR description gives a reviewer the most to act on?
options: "About 20% faster on my machine."
"Encode is 17.2% faster (median of 10 interleaved runs each, p=0.000 via benchstat, idle linux/amd64); cache adds one entry per type."
"Encode is much faster now; see the flame graph screenshot."
"Benchmarks pass in CI, so performance is fine."
explain: Only the second states the method (10 interleaved runs, median), a significance result, the setup, and the cost. The others give no way to judge noise or to rerun the experiment, and "CI passes" usually checks correctness, not speed.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
question: You run `git grep -n parse_config` in a project and get no hits, but you can see `parse_config` in a file in your editor. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The file is untracked or ignored, and git grep searches tracked files only
git grep is case-insensitive by default
git grep needs `-r` to search subdirectories
git grep only searches the last commit, not the working tree
explain: By default git grep searches tracked files in the working tree. A new file you have not added, or one matched by .gitignore, is invisible to it. Use `--untracked` (and `--no-exclude-standard` for ignored files). Recursion is already the default, and the working tree, not HEAD, is searched.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
question: Which of these is the strongest version of the *Reproducible* property?
options: You copied the failing lines out of your app into the report
You described the steps carefully from memory
You ran the exact snippet in the report in a fresh environment and saw the same error
explain: Reproducible means tested. Copying lines out of a larger program often drops something they depended on, and memory is unreliable. Stack Overflow's guide suggests transporting the example to a fresh environment to confirm it still fails, because you may have accidentally fixed or changed the bug while trimming.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
question: A contributor's PR adds a new public function `parse_duration()` but no caller, promising "the caller comes in the next PR". What is the strongest review concern?
options: The PR is too large and should be split further
The PR is too small to judge: without a use, reviewers cannot tell if the API is right
New functions always need a separate design document first
It should be a draft because it has no tests
explain: Google's guide on small CLs (changelists, Google's internal name for a change sent for review, like a PR) says a change should not be so small that its implications are hard to understand; adding an API with a usage lets reviewers see how it will be used and avoids checking in unused APIs.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
question: A kernel reads the KV of position `pos` at `base + pos * bytes_per_token`, as a contiguous kernel would. After switching to paged storage, what goes wrong?
options: It reads the right tokens only while the sequence fits in its first block; later positions land in whatever block happens to sit next in memory
Nothing, because physical blocks are allocated in increasing order
It reads correct data but more slowly
It fails only for requests that share blocks
explain: Logical blocks are mapped to arbitrary physical blocks (7, 1, 3 in the example). Only offsets inside a block are contiguous, so every access must go through the block table: `table[pos // B] * B + pos % B`.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Prefill on top of a cached prefix, and sharing the compute too
question: 32 requests share a 4,000-token prompt through shared paged blocks, stored once. During decoding, why does attention still move about 32 prefixes' worth of KV per step?
options: Copy-on-write duplicates the prefix at the first decode step
The block table has to be copied once per request
Each request's query runs its own matrix-vector product, which loads the shared blocks itself; sharing removed duplicate storage, not duplicate reads
Prefix caching is switched off during decoding
explain: Copy-on-write only copies a shared block that someone writes into, and prefix blocks are full and never written. The shared blocks stay single copies, but a per-request decode kernel reads them once per request. Cascade inference or Hydragen batch the 32 queries against the prefix so it is read once.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
question: A client asks you to test their online shop, which runs on a large hosted e-commerce platform. The client has signed your permission to test. What is still missing?
options: Nothing: the client's signature covers everything the shop uses
Checking the platform's own security testing policy, because the client cannot authorise testing of the provider's systems
A faster scanner
Permission from the shop's customers
explain: PTES: the client does not speak for third-party providers. Many platforms publish testing rules or bug bounty scopes; only what they allow can be tested, and only the client's own parts.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
question: A team issues individual certificates for `vpn`, `jira-test` and `payroll-old` under their domain. What does Certificate Transparency mean for them?
options: Nothing, because certificates are private between the CA and the company
Those names are permanently in public append-only logs, so each host must be secured as if everyone knows it exists
The names are hidden unless someone guesses them
CT only logs expired certificates
explain: CT logs are public and append-only, and Chrome requires publicly trusted certificates to be logged. Anyone can search them, so obscure names give no protection.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Web enumeration: crawling, content discovery and fingerprinting
question: During discovery `/admin/` returns 403 and `/admin-old/` returns 404. What do you report?
options: Both paths exist
Neither path exists
/admin/ exists and refuses access (worth checking whether it is meant to be reachable at all); /admin-old/ appears not to exist
/admin-old/ is hidden better and is more dangerous
explain: 403 means the server knows the resource and refuses it; 404 means it found nothing (unless the app masks codes). An admin path reachable from the internet, even if refusing, is worth reviewing.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Attack surface management: recon as a defender
question: Which control would most directly have prevented a server from becoming one of the 32,820 wiped MongoDB databases?
options: A stronger ransom-negotiation policy
Encrypting the database files on disk
A longer password on the operating system's root account
Not exposing port 27017 to the internet and enabling MongoDB access control, verified by an external scan
explain: The attacks needed only network reachability and no authentication. Disk encryption does nothing against a logged-in database client; binding locally, firewalling and enabling auth do.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
question: In a flame graph, `json_encode` is 300 px wide but the boxes on top of it cover 290 px. What does that tell you?
options: json_encode itself is the hot spot; optimize its loop
json_encode was called 300 times
Almost all of json_encode's time is in the functions it calls; it executes very little itself
json_encode ran during the first quarter of the profile
explain: Only the exposed top edge (10 px) is self time. The other 290 px belong to its callees. Width says nothing about call counts, and x position says nothing about when.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
question: Spot the bug: `n->key = k; n->next = old; clwb(n); head = n; clwb(&head); sfence();` (n fits in one line; head is in another line).
options: Nothing: the final sfence orders everything before it
CLWB should be CLFLUSH, because CLWB keeps the line in cache so it is not durable
The sfence must come between clwb(n) and head = n; otherwise head can be durable before the node
head must be written with a non-temporal store
explain: The single trailing fence only guarantees both lines are durable at the end. Before it, head = n may be evicted or written back first, giving the head-only crash state. CLWB keeping a clean copy in cache is fine: the data was written back.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
question: IC3 2025 shows about 191,561 phishing complaints and 24,768 BEC complaints, but BEC losses are about 14 times larger. What best explains this?
options: Phishing is often the entry step, while BEC is where large wire transfers are lost
BEC victims exaggerate their losses
Phishing has stopped causing any losses
BEC complaints are counted in a different currency
explain: Phishing is the common first step: it steals passwords or opens conversations. BEC is the monetising step, where a single fraudulent wire can be millions. The categories overlap, so the totals are a rough picture, not exact accounting.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
question: Why can receiving servers not simply reject every message whose envelope-from differs from its header From?
options: Because SMTP forbids comparing them
Because the header From is encrypted
Because envelope-from is always empty
Because mailing services legitimately use their own bounce address while sending as a brand's From address
explain: Bulk senders, ticketing systems and forwarders routinely use a different envelope-from to collect bounces. DMARC solves this with alignment rules that allow related domains instead of demanding an exact match everywhere.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message
question: A message has two Authentication-Results headers: the top from mx.corp.example (dmarc=fail) and a lower one from mx.corp.example (dmarc=pass). Which do you trust?
options: The lower one, because it is older and closer to the sender
The top one, because it was added by your border server on arrival
Neither; Authentication-Results are always forged
Both; take the more favourable
explain: Your border server prepends its result on arrival, so the top one carrying your own authserv-id is yours. Anything lower was written before your server got the message. RFC 8601 says such forged copies should be deleted by the border server.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and why passkeys resist it
question: After an AiTM incident, the help desk resets the victim's password. Why is that not enough?
options: Passwords cannot be reset remotely
The attacker's stolen session cookie may stay valid until sessions are revoked
The attacker also needs the new password to keep reading mail
Password resets delete the mailbox
explain: The attacker never needed the password after login; the cookie is the access. Revoke sessions and tokens, remove attacker-added MFA methods and inbox rules, then reset.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
question: What is `sizeof(union U)` for `union U { char s[13]; int i; };` on x86-64?
explain: A union's size is its largest member, 13 bytes for s, rounded up to the union's alignment, which is 4 because of i. 13 rounded up to a multiple of 4 is 16. 17 would add the members instead of overlapping them.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Strict aliasing: which pointer casts C lets you read through
question: Which of these reads of `double d = 2.0;` is defined behavior in C?
options: `unsigned char b0 = *(unsigned char *)&d;`
`long bits = *(long *)&d;` (both 8 bytes, alignment 8)
`int lo = *(int *)&d;`
`float f = *(float *)&d;`
explain: Character types may read any object, so reading one byte of d through `unsigned char *` is fine. long has the same size and alignment as double here, but size and alignment do not matter to the aliasing rule: only the types on the list in 6.5 paragraph 7 may read a double.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
question: A C library takes `double` arguments in meters. You wrap them in Rust as `struct Meters(f64);`. Which attribute guarantees a `Meters` is passed exactly like an `f64`?
options: #[repr(C)]
#[repr(transparent)]
#[repr(packed)]
None: a one-field struct is always passed like its field
explain: repr(transparent) gives the struct the layout and ABI of its single non-zero-sized field. repr(C) promises C struct layout, but the Reference notes a C struct's ABI can differ from the bare field's; the default repr promises nothing.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
question: A squat-depth checker flags every rep as too shallow, but only for users who film from directly in front. What is the most likely cause?
options: The OKS sigma for knees is too large
Foreshortening: in a frontal 2D view the thigh points at the camera, so the 2D knee angle looks straighter than it is
The heatmap resolution is too low
Hysteresis thresholds are too far apart
explain: A 2D angle measures the projection. When thigh or shin points toward the camera, it shrinks in the image and the projected angle opens up (111 degrees in 3D looked like 173 in the example). OKS sigmas only affect evaluation.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
question: Why did NIST select HQC in March 2025 when ML-KEM was already standardised?
options: HQC is faster and smaller than ML-KEM
Because HQC is the only KEM approved for hybrids
Because ML-KEM was broken
As a backup based on different math (error-correcting codes), in case a weakness is found in ML-KEM
explain: NIST's announcement calls HQC a second line of defence and says ML-KEM remains the recommended choice. Cloudflare's 2025 review adds that HQC is larger and slower on every metric, so it is insurance rather than a replacement.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: KyberSlash: when one division leaks the key
question: Which deployment was most exposed to KyberSlash?
options: A browser doing hybrid TLS with a fresh key share per connection
A laptop verifying ML-DSA signatures
A server that only encapsulates to clients' keys
An embedded device with one long-term Kyber decapsulation key that decapsulates ciphertexts from anyone on the network
explain: The attack needs many timed decapsulations under the same secret key. Ephemeral TLS keys block that; a static key reachable by attackers does not.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Rolling it out: browsers, middleboxes and big certificates
question: Roughly how many extra bytes would ML-DSA-44 add to the authentication part of a first TLS visit (5 signatures, 2 public keys), compared with ECDSA P-256?
options: About 1.5 kB
None: signature sizes are similar
About 150 kB
About 15 kB
explain: 5 x 2420 + 2 x 1312 = 14,724 bytes versus about 450, so roughly 14 kB more. This is the 'second migration' problem that Merkle Tree Certificates aim to solve.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
question: An engineer says: pre-filtering is always exact, so it is always better than post-filtering. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, exactness always wins
Pre-filtering cannot handle AND conditions
Its flat-scan cost is s n distances, which at broad filters is close to a full scan; post-filtering a graph search is far cheaper when most vectors match
Pre-filtering returns fewer than k results when s is small
explain: Exactness is not free. At s = 0.6 on 50 million vectors, a flat scan does 30 million distance computations, while post-filtering loses little (60% of candidates survive) at graph-search cost. Pre-filtering never under-fills: it returns k whenever at least k vectors match.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Measure it: recall and cost versus selectivity
question: Faiss HNSW with an IDSelector returns 1.56 of 10 results at s = 0.005, while the same graph with no filter returns 10. Why?
options: The selector is checked only when adding results; the walk is the unfiltered one, so only matches among the roughly 345 nodes it scores on the bottom layer can be returned
IDSelectorBitmap only works with IVF indexes
The selector makes Faiss skip non-matching nodes, which disconnects the graph
Faiss caps filtered results at k times s
explain: In Faiss's HNSW.cpp every neighbor is pushed onto the candidate queue regardless of the selector; the selector gates only the result heap. The walk is the same as unfiltered: 390.5 distances, about 345 of them on the bottom layer where results are collected, so at s = 0.005 about 1.7 of those nodes match. Raising efSearch widens the walk.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall
question: A loop reads two cache lines sequentially, then jumps to a random place and reads two lines again, and so on. Why does the hardware prefetcher help very little here?
options: Prefetchers only work on writes
The prefetcher requires 64 consecutive lines before starting
Random jumps disable the cache
After the two misses that train it, the stream ends, so its predictions point at lines that will never be read
explain: Training takes about two misses, and by then this short run is over. The prefetcher's guesses past the end become wasted bandwidth, the same overshoot Intel's manual warns about for short arrays.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Linking attacks: ZIP code, birth date and sex
question: One attribute value is shared by 1 in 1,024 people. How many bits of identifying information does it carry?
options: 10 bits
1 bit
1,024 bits
It depends on encryption
explain: Surprisal is log2(1/p) = log2(1024) = 10 bits. Bits from independent attributes add, which is why a few ordinary attributes together single people out.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: When k-anonymity fails: l-diversity and t-closeness
question: A class has 10 records: 9 'HIV positive' and 1 'HIV negative'. The whole table is 2 percent positive. Which property does this class satisfy, and why is it still a problem?
options: It fails k-anonymity because k must exceed 10
It satisfies t-closeness because both values appear
It is safe because no row can be identified
It is distinct 2-diverse, but membership raises the estimate from 2 to 90 percent (a skewness attack)
explain: Two distinct values make it distinct 2-diverse, but the class distribution (90 percent) is far from the table's (2 percent), so t-closeness fails. Knowing someone is in the class tells you they are very likely positive.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Case: the 2020 US Census adopts differential privacy
question: Why could the 2010 Census tables leak individual records even though only aggregate tables were published?
options: The tables were sent unencrypted
Swapping published the original records
The tables included names
Many exact, overlapping tables form a system of constraints that only a few (sometimes one) sets of records satisfy
explain: Each exact table is a constraint. Enough constraints pin down the records, as the three-person block shows. Noise with a budget limits how much the constraints can reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Secure aggregation: a server that learns only the sum
question: In the pairwise masking scheme, why does the server learn nothing from a single masked value y_u?
options: Because y_u includes uniformly random pair secrets the server does not know, which act as a one-time pad on x_u
Because y_u is encrypted with TLS
Because the server deletes y_u after summing
Because x_u is always small
explain: Adding a uniformly random value mod R is a one-time pad: y_u is uniformly distributed whatever x_u is. Only the sum, where the pads cancel, carries information.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: After the foothold: the four tactics defenders must see
question: An intruder on a workstation runs built-in commands that list domain admins, domain controllers and open file shares. Which ATT&CK tactic is this?
options: Privilege Escalation (TA0004)
Discovery (TA0007)
Lateral Movement (TA0008)
Credential Access (TA0006)
explain: Listing accounts, servers and shares is Discovery: learning the environment. No privilege changed, no credential was taken and no other machine was entered yet, although the results guide all three.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions
question: Which right on a service object, granted to ordinary users, amounts to giving them SYSTEM?
options: SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS
SERVICE_INTERROGATE
SERVICE_ENUMERATE_DEPENDENTS
SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG
explain: SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG lets the holder change the executable the service runs; Microsoft says it should be granted only to administrators. The other three only read status or dependency information.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credential hygiene: LAPS, Credential Guard, tiers and JIT admin
question: Which control directly stops a local Administrator hash stolen from one laptop being reused on the other 499?
options: Credential Guard
Protected Users group
Remote Credential Guard
Windows LAPS
explain: LAPS gives every device its own rotating local admin password, so the stolen hash is valid on one machine only. Credential Guard protects domain credentials in LSASS, not local SAM hashes; Protected Users is for domain accounts; Remote Credential Guard protects RDP sessions.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
question: A generator samples 100 solutions to a hard olympiad problem; 97 have wrong final answers. Why is outcome supervision on this problem a weak training signal for a reward model?
options: Outcome labels are noisy because the answer checker is usually wrong
Almost every label is 0, and a 0 does not say which step failed, so the model learns little about where reasoning breaks
Outcome labels cannot be computed for olympiad problems
The reward model would overfit to the 3 correct solutions and ignore the rest
explain: When nearly all solutions are wrong, a 0 is the expected label and says only 'some step was wrong'. Lightman et al. make exactly this credit-assignment argument: process labels also say how many leading steps were right and where the first mistake is.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: What should a step reward measure? Value, progress, implicit PRMs
question: In an implicit PRM, what is the step reward for step t?
options: The PRM's sigmoid output at the step's last token
The sum of beta log(pi_theta / pi_ref) over the tokens inside step t, which equals the change in the soft Q value across the step
The fraction of reference-model rollouts from step t that reach the right answer
beta times the step's length in tokens
explain: The running sum of token log ratios is a soft Q value of the prefix (Yuan et al., Proposition 3.1). Its change across a step, which is the sum of the token terms inside the step, is the step's process reward. No rollouts or step labels are needed.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a process owns and what a thread shares
question: Thread A in a process opens a file and gets file descriptor 5. Thread B, in the same process, calls `read(5, buf, 100)` without opening anything. What happens?
options: It fails with EBADF (the bad file descriptor error), because descriptors are private to the thread that opened them
It reads from the same open file, because threads share the process's descriptor table
It reads from a fresh copy of the file starting at offset 0
It blocks until thread A closes the descriptor
explain: The descriptor table is a process resource, so every thread in the process sees fd 5 and the same file offset. Only per-thread state is private: registers, stack, thread ID, and the signal mask.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
question: Two CPU-bound threads share one core: one at nice 0 (weight 1024) and one at nice 1 (weight 820). Roughly what share does the nice 0 thread get?
options: 50 percent: nice only matters when there is spare CPU
90 percent: each nice level is a 10x factor
100 percent: the nice 1 thread waits until the nice 0 thread blocks
explain: Shares follow weights: 1024/1844 = 55.5 percent against 44.5. One nice level is a factor of about 1.25, which works out to roughly 10 percent of CPU moving between the two tasks.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
question: You use m = 16 sub-quantizers with k* = 256 on 512-dim float32 vectors. How many bytes does each PQ code take, and what is the compression ratio?
options: 16 bytes, 128x smaller than 2,048 bytes
256 bytes, 8x smaller
64 bytes, because each sub-vector stores 32 dims
2 bytes, because 16 codes x 1 bit
explain: Each of the 16 indices takes log2(256) = 8 bits = 1 byte, so 16 bytes. The raw vector is 512 x 4 = 2,048 bytes, so the ratio is 128x. The sub-vector width (32 dims) changes the codebook size, not the code size.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
question: Your team tuned a prompt by hand to 91% on model X. Leadership switches to model Y. What does the evidence in this lesson suggest?
options: The prompt will keep roughly its 91% because its meaning has not changed
Re-run the search on model Y with the same metric and dev set, because the best prompt and format are model-specific
Add "You are an expert" to the prompt, since personas transfer across models
Only the few-shot examples need changing, never the instruction
explain: Sclar et al. found format performance only weakly correlates between models, and on GSM8K the APE trigger beat "Let's think step by step." with InstructGPT (43.0% versus 40.7%) but lost with PaLM 2-L (58.8% versus 71.8%). Keep the metric and data, and re-optimize for the new model.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
question: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock's simple prompt optimization matches the AWS docs?
options: It searches over many candidates and returns the one with the best score on your data
It performs a fast heuristic rewrite of one prompt for one chosen model and does not use evaluation data
It fine-tunes the target model on your prompt
It guarantees the rewritten prompt scores higher on your task
explain: The docs describe simple optimization as a heuristic rewrite of a single short prompt for one model, with no evaluation data and no multi-model support. Evaluation-driven optimization is the separate Advanced Prompt Optimization feature.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations
question: At the start of sampling, what is the distribution of a residue's orientation?
options: The orientation of the nearest residue in the training set
Close to uniform on SO(3): all orientations equally likely, mean pairwise angle about 126.5 degrees
Identity, because the noise schedule starts from the identity rotation
A Maxwell density with scale 0.45 radians
explain: The large-t limit of IGSO(3) is the uniform (Haar) measure on SO(3). The computed mean angle at t = 4.0 is 124.5 degrees, already within 2 degrees of the uniform limit of 126.5, and the L1 distance between the two densities is 0.045.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
question: Which line correctly opens a log so that one invalid byte cannot stop the script?
options: open(path)
open(path, "rb")
open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
open(path, encoding="ascii")
explain: With `errors="replace"` invalid bytes become the replacement character and reading continues. `"rb"` would avoid decoding entirely but then every line is `bytes`, not text, and string methods with `str` arguments fail. ASCII would reject any non-ASCII byte.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: HTTP and REST APIs: making requests safely
question: Your enrichment script calls `requests.get(url, headers=h)` with no timeout. One night the provider's load balancer (the front server that spreads requests across its machines) accepts connections but stops answering. What happens?
options: Requests gives up after its default 30-second timeout
Python raises ConnectionError immediately
The operating system retries on another server
The call can wait indefinitely, so the job hangs and no error is reported
explain: Requests has no default timeout. A connection that is open but silent can block the call indefinitely, which in a scheduled job looks like "still running" rather than "failed". Always pass `timeout=`.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
question: Which of these is a *local* method in the Manning et al. sense?
options: A synonym file mapping car to automobile
Looking up each query word in WordNet
Extracting frequent terms from the top 10 results and re-querying with them
Lowercasing and stemming the query
explain: Local methods adjust the query using the documents it initially retrieves (pseudo-relevance feedback here). Synonym files and WordNet are global: they expand the same way regardless of results. Stemming is ordinary analysis, applied to documents and queries alike.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
question: Why does query2doc repeat the query 5 times before appending the pseudo-document for BM25?
options: To keep the original terms from being outweighed by the much longer generated passage
To raise the query's IDF
Because BM25 ignores terms that appear only once in a query
To force the LLM to stay on topic
explain: BM25 over a long concatenated query is a sum over many terms; without repetition the passage's words dominate. Repeating q is a weight on the original terms, like the 0.5 weight on synonyms or RM3's original query weight.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Decomposition: Self-Ask, least-to-most and sub-query evidence
question: Self-Ask stops generation at `Intermediate answer:` before calling search. What would go wrong if it let the model keep generating?
options: The model would write its own intermediate answer from memory, which can be a hallucination the search was meant to replace
The prompt would exceed the context window immediately
The search engine would receive the final answer instead of the question
Nothing; stopping only saves tokens
explain: Stopping right before the answer slot is what makes room for retrieved evidence. Without the stop, the model fills the slot itself, and the search result, if added later, conflicts with text the model already conditioned on.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
question: Why does RaBitQ apply P^-1 to each data vector instead of rotating the codebook?
options: Rotating 2^D codewords is impossible to store or search; rotating one vector and reading its signs finds the same nearest codeword
P^-1 is cheaper to compute than P
The codebook must stay axis-aligned for popcount to work
It makes the code shorter than D bits
explain: Inner products are invariant under rotation, so maximizing over P x is the same as maximizing over x against P^-1 o, which is solved by copying signs. The codebook stays conceptual.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
question: Which of these is a business logic flaw rather than an injection or configuration bug?
options: A search box passes its input into an SQL query, so a quote character causes a database error
A shop grants a threshold discount when the code is entered and keeps it after items are removed
A server still accepts TLS 1.0 connections
A comment field renders HTML tags from other users
explain: The discount bug breaks no technical rule: each request is valid and the code does what it was told. The rule (discount only while the cart is 1000 or more) was checked at the wrong time. The others are injection, protocol configuration and cross-site scripting.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
question: In the lost-update variant, five withdrawals of 100 succeed and the final balance reads 0. Why is this worse than ending at -400?
options: The balance looks valid, so nothing flags the 400 paid out without funds until payouts are reconciled
It is not worse, both lose the same amount
Because 0 cannot be stored in the database
Because the user can withdraw again
explain: With -400, an obvious invariant (balance never negative) is visibly broken. With 0, the account looks normal and the loss hides in the difference between recorded payouts and the balance, which only reconciliation finds.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
question: An app uses SERIALIZABLE isolation and logs SQLSTATE 40001 errors but returns them to users as "transfer failed". What is missing?
options: Nothing, a failed transfer is the safe outcome
A switch back to Read Committed
A retry of the whole transaction from the beginning, as PostgreSQL's documentation requires
A FOR UPDATE on every SELECT
explain: Serialization failures are expected under SERIALIZABLE; the database aborted one transaction to keep the result consistent. Retrying the whole transaction gives honest users their transfer (and a racing duplicate a correct refusal). Returning the error is safe but makes ordinary concurrent use fail.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to logic and race abuse
question: A wallet balance reads 0 and no alert fired, but its ledger sums to -400. Which detection caught the problem, and what kind of race left it?
options: A burst rule; a limit overrun with a negative balance
A web application firewall (WAF) signature; SQL injection
Reconciliation of balance against ledger; a lost update, where later writes overwrote earlier ones
A rate limit; credential stuffing
explain: The balance itself looks valid, so only comparing it with the ledger reveals the gap. A lost update (writing a value computed from a stale read) produces exactly this: five recorded payouts, one visible debit.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
question: A follower's log has entries with terms [1, 1, 2] at indexes 1 to 3. It receives AppendEntries with prevLogIndex = 3, prevLogTerm = 3 and one new entry. What happens?
options: It appends the entry at index 4
It overwrites entry 3 with term 3 and appends
It rejects; the leader will retry with a smaller nextIndex
It starts an election because the leader looks stale
explain: The follower's entry 3 has term 2, not 3, so the consistency check fails and it refuses the request. The leader decrements nextIndex and retries until it finds the last index where both logs agree; only then are conflicting entries replaced.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
question: Why did overlap 4 make the People team fact retrievable as one chunk in D1?
options: Overlap makes the embedding model weight the last words of a chunk higher
Overlap removes stopwords at chunk boundaries
Overlap guarantees every sentence is whole in exactly one chunk
With windows starting every 8 words, S6 (words 34 to 44) fits wholly inside the window covering words 32 to 44
explain: Overlap does not guarantee anything about sentences; it only shifts where windows start. Here the shifted window D1.5 happens to contain all of S6. A sentence longer than the stride can still be cut in every window, which is why structure-aware splitters exist.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: The seven failure points and how to debug them
question: Logs show the correct chunk at rank 2 from the retriever, but it never appears in the final prompt because the prompt builder deduplicates by document and keeps only the first chunk per document. Which failure point is this?
options: FP 2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
FP 3 Not in Context
FP 4 Not Extracted
FP 1 Missing Content
explain: Retrieval succeeded: the chunk ranked 2nd. It was lost during consolidation into the context, which is FP 3. Raising k would not help; the consolidation rule has to change.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
question: You fit min-max normalization on last month's training data (views max 95000). Today a document has 400000 views. What does the serving-time normalizer produce, and is that a problem?
options: Exactly 1.0, nothing to worry about
An error, because the value is out of range
0, because unknown values default to zero
About 4.2, outside the range the model was trained on
explain: Min-max uses the stored constants: (400000 - 12) / (95000 - 12) is about 4.2. A linear model extrapolates past anything it saw; a tree treats it like the largest training value. Clipping, log transforms or rank-based encodings make this less surprising.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
question: You switch your nDCG@10 code from log2 to natural log in the discount, keeping everything else fixed. What happens to the scores?
options: Every nDCG@10 changes by the factor ln 2
Nothing: the constant factor cancels between DCG and ideal DCG
Ranks 1 and 2 become undiscounted
nDCG can now exceed 1
explain: log_e(i+1) = ln 2 times log2(i+1) for every rank, so both the run's DCG and the ideal DCG are scaled by the same factor 1/ln 2, which cancels. Raw DCG does change, and so does the original Jarvelin-Kekalainen form, where the base also decides how many ranks escape discounting.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: A crime with a supply chain: the roles and the money
question: Why did LockBit advertise that its affiliates receive the ransom first and then send the core its cut?
options: It reduced the affiliate's risk of being cheated by the core, which helped recruit affiliates
It let LockBit avoid sanctions because the core never touched the money
It was required by the cryptocurrency exchanges the group used
It made the payment untraceable for law enforcement
explain: CISA lists it among LockBit's ways to attract affiliates, in contrast to groups that pay themselves first. Affiliates carry the risk of the intrusion and fear not being paid; who holds the money first decides who can cheat whom. It does not affect sanctions or traceability.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Inside: from one login to Domain Admin to the hypervisor
question: Why did CVE-2024-37085 let any domain user who could create groups become an ESXi administrator?
options: ESXi stored the root password in AD
Domain users are local admins on ESXi by default
ESXi trusted a group by its name, so a newly created group called ESX Admins was given full admin rights
The group's SID was hard-coded in ESXi
explain: Microsoft found that domain-joined ESXi granted full admin to members of a group named ESX Admins, without checking that the group existed beforehand and matching it by name, not SID. Creating the group with that name was enough.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Hardening that actually blocks the path
question: An organisation enforces MFA on its VPN, but its ESXi hosts take admin rights from AD. An attacker phishes a help desk into resetting an employee's MFA and later becomes domain admin. Which control from the matrix would still stop mass VM encryption?
options: Phishing-resistant MFA on the VPN
Egress baselining
Approved RMM only
ESXi admin authentication separated from AD, with lockdown mode
explain: Once AD is owned, any system that trusts AD for admin rights falls with it. ESXi hosts with local, per-host credentials and lockdown mode do not. The other controls address earlier steps the attacker already passed.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
question: You already use `sendfile` so the server never copies file bytes into user space. Which cost does RDMA remove that `sendfile` still pays?
options: Running the transport protocol and a system call on the host CPU for each message
The copy from the page cache into a socket buffer
The DMA from host memory to the NIC
The need to know the destination address
explain: `sendfile` already avoids the user-space copy, and DMA between memory and the NIC happens in both designs. What stays with sockets is the kernel: a system call per operation and the TCP stack running on a CPU per packet. RDMA moves the transport into the NIC and lets the application post work without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
question: You want one server to accept requests from 10,000 clients with as little NIC state as possible. Which transport fits, and what does it give up?
options: UD: one QP can talk to every client, but only SEND/RECV of at most one MTU per message
RC: it supports every verb
UC: it is unreliable, so it needs no state
UD: it supports RDMA READ without connections
explain: A connected QP (RC or UC) talks to exactly one peer, so 10,000 clients need 10,000 QPs. A UD QP can exchange datagrams with any UD QP, which is why designs like HERD use it for responses. The price: no RDMA READ/WRITE or atomics, no reliability, and single-MTU messages.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
question: A server receives a client frame whose MASK bit is 0. What does RFC 6455 require?
options: Close the connection, optionally with close code 1002 (protocol error)
Unmask it with a zero key and process it normally
Reply with a ping to ask the client to resend it masked
Accept it only if the connection is over TLS
explain: Section 5.1: the server MUST close the connection on an unmasked client frame and MAY send close code 1002. Masking is required whether or not TLS is used, so TLS does not make it optional.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: Your game streams 20 snapshots per second over WebSocket at 150 ms RTT on a lossy mobile link. Players see enemies freeze then jump. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Enable TCP_NODELAY on the server
Move snapshots to an unreliable channel such as WebTransport datagrams, keeping reliable messages on a stream
Lower the patch rate to 5 per second
Switch from t.float32() to t.number()
explain: The freeze-then-burst pattern is head-of-line blocking: a lost packet holds back later snapshots until retransmission. TCP_NODELAY only disables Nagle batching. An unreliable channel lets newer snapshots through, and the interpolation buffer skips the gap.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
question: A two-tower model trained with plain in-batch softmax rarely retrieves the top-100 hit items, even for users who like them. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hit items appear in many batches, so they are used as negatives far more often and get pushed down; apply the logQ correction
The temperature is too high, so all scores are equal
Hit items have too few training examples
Normalizing embeddings removes popularity information
explain: In-batch negatives follow the traffic distribution, which is power-law: a few hits take most of the traffic. Yi et al. note popular items are overly penalized as negatives and subtract log p_j from each logit to correct the bias.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Rectifying the plane: card corners to millimeters
question: A colleague fits H from the card corners, but lists the mm points in the order TL, BL, BR, TR while the pixel points are TL, TR, BR, BL. What happens?
options: H maps the card onto a transposed card, so lengths along the card's width and height are swapped and measurements are wrong
OpenCV automatically sorts the points, so nothing changes
The fit fails with an error because the points are not in clockwise order
Only the sign of the result flips
explain: The solver trusts the pairing you give it. Swapped pairs still define a valid homography, just to a wrong rectangle (85.6 placed along the 53.98 side), so it returns confidently wrong numbers. This is why ArUco returns corners in a fixed order.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
question: For parallel aggregation, two workers compute partial results for group a. Worker 1 saw 30; worker 2 saw 50 and 40. What should the final step combine to get avg = 40?
options: The two averages, 30 and 45, averaged to 37.5
The two states (1, 30) and (2, 90), added to (3, 120), then 120 / 3
Only the larger worker's average, 45
The two averages weighted equally, then rounded
explain: Averaging averages gives 37.5, which is wrong. The correct merge combines transition states: counts add and sums add, then the final function divides once. PostgreSQL supports this with combine functions for partial aggregation; the merge works on states, not on finished results.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Latency: you wait for the slowest replica you need
question: N = 5, replica delays independent with the same distribution. Which choice gives the lowest 99.9th percentile write latency while still overlapping reads done with R = 3?
explain: Overlap needs $R + W > 5$, so with R = 3 the smallest valid W is 3. Latency only grows with W (you wait for a later order statistic), so W = 3 is the fastest correct choice. W = 1 or 2 is faster but breaks the overlap.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
question: Same house, true reward [1, 1, 1]. A new proxy over-weights the attic: [3, 1, 1]. Using the 8 deterministic policies, is it hackable?
options: No: it gives positive weight to every room, so it agrees with the true reward
Yes: A alone gets proxy 3 but true 1, while B+K gets proxy 2 but true 2
No: over-weighting one room only changes ties, never strict orderings
Yes, but only for stochastic policies
explain: The proxy prefers A (3 over 2) while the true reward prefers B+K (2 over 1): a strict reversal. Positive weights on every room are not enough. A milder proxy [2, 1, 1] would tie A with B+K (2 and 2) and, by exhaustive check, has no strict reversal.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Fixing the reward, not just the leash: ensembles, WARM, ODIN, PAR
question: You can train five reward models but afford only one reward-model forward pass per sample during RL. Which method fits?
options: A prediction ensemble with worst-case combination
A prediction ensemble with UWO
Train five RMs from scratch with different random seeds and average their weights
WARM: fine-tune five RMs from the same SFT model and average their weights
explain: Both prediction ensembles need five forward passes per sample. Weight averaging gives one model, but only works when the members share pretraining (linear mode connectivity); RMs trained from scratch do not stay connected, so their average is a broken model.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
question: A developer finds that the production admin console has no multi-factor login. Under the Three Lines Model, who should decide whether to accept or fix this risk?
options: The developer, because they found it
Internal audit, because it is independent
The risk owner of the system, within their delegated authority, advised by the CISO's team
The external auditor at the next audit
explain: First-line owners own and decide on their risks, with second-line advice and challenge. Internal audit stays independent precisely so it can later judge that decision; external auditors only report.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
question: After mitigation the residual ALE is USD 256,000 and the board's appetite allows that. What should happen next?
options: Nothing; the risk is closed
The residual risk must be transferred to insurance
The risk owner formally accepts the residual risk, recorded in the register with a review date
Mitigate until residual risk is zero
explain: Residual risk is never zero. It is accepted explicitly by someone with the authority to do so, and reviewed on a schedule.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
question: A vendor offers a SOC 2 Type I report dated 14 months ago. What does it tell you?
options: That its controls were suitably designed and in place on one date 14 months ago, and nothing about whether they operated since
That its controls worked for the last 14 months
That it is ISO 27001 certified
That it passed a PCI assessment
explain: Type I is a point-in-time design opinion. For operating effectiveness you need a Type II covering a recent period, plus a bridge letter for the gap since the period ended.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
question: Which NIS2 article makes management bodies approve and oversee cybersecurity risk-management measures and allows them to be held liable?
options: Article 20
Article 23
Article 21
Article 34
explain: Article 20 covers governance: approval, oversight, liability and mandatory training for management. Article 21 lists the measures, 23 the reporting, 34 the fines.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
question: With a USD 250,000 deductible and a USD 3 million limit, how much does the company bear in a year with a USD 2 million loss?
options: USD 0
explain: The company pays the first 250,000; the insurer pays the remaining 1.75 million, which is within the limit.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: A colleague proposes doubling the number of rollout engines, each still decoding a share of one synchronous batch, to fix 51% engine idleness. What is the main flaw?
options: More engines need more weight-sync bandwidth, which is the real bottleneck
Doubling engines doubles the length of every response
Engines cannot run in parallel on one batch
The idle time is set by the longest response, and one response cannot be split across engines, so the phase still lasts as long as that response
explain: Autoregressive decoding of one response is sequential. Adding engines shortens the time to finish the short responses, but the phase still waits for the longest one, so idleness goes up. verl's fully async docs make the same point: in the colocated case, adding rollout resources cannot remove long-tail idleness.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: NeMo RL async GRPO runs with max_trajectory_age_steps: 1. A trajectory was generated with weights v10. At which training steps can it be used?
options: Steps 10 and 11; at step 12 it is discarded
Only step 10
Steps 9, 10 and 11
Any step, as long as importance sampling correction is on
explain: The docs' own example: a trajectory generated with v10 can be used for training steps v10 or v11, and at step v12 it is too old and is discarded. Importance correction handles the remaining mismatch; it does not remove the age limit.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
question: In the toy model, tool waits grow from 1 to 20 s to 10 to 60 s. Which change keeps the inference GPUs busiest?
options: Batch per turn with a larger batch
A tighter maximum response length
Move tools onto the GPU servers
Run many more concurrent trajectories as independent coroutines, so some are always decoding while others wait on tools
explain: With independent loops, GPU idleness comes only from too few trajectories being ready to decode. More concurrent trajectories fill the gaps, which is what Kimi K2 does with a large number of concurrent rollouts; batch per turn keeps a global idle phase for every tool round.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: The four golden signals, read as distributions
question: Which single measurement best distinguishes the hypothesis that catalog is itself saturated from the hypothesis that catalog's database got slow?
options: Catalog's p99 latency, which is 1000 ms either way
Catalog's error rate of 7.41 percent
The number of catalog pods firing alerts
Catalog's pool wait time against its database query time: 988 ms waiting for a connection versus 12 ms executing the query
explain: p99, error rate and alert count are identical under both hypotheses, so none of them discriminates. Splitting the latency into time spent waiting for a resource and time spent doing work does: the query still takes 12 ms, so the database is fine and the backlog is in front of the pool. Instrument the wait and the work separately, or you cannot tell these apart during an incident.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
question: Your organisation writes excellent postmortems and the same class of incident keeps recurring. Which measurement would tell you where the process is leaking?
options: Mean time to resolution for the recurring class
Number of postmortems written per quarter
The fraction of action items with an owner, a bug and a priority that were completed, broken down by type
Number of alerts fired per incident
explain: Writing the document is not the mechanism that reduces recurrence; completing the typed, owned, tracked items is. Counting postmortems measures effort, and MTTR measures response rather than prevention. If completion is low, the leak is in prioritisation; if completion is high and recurrence continues, the items are not naming the right conditions.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: You are writing a Rust driver and need a C function from a subsystem that has no Rust abstraction yet. What does kernel policy expect?
options: Call it through `bindings::` inside an `unsafe` block in the driver, with a SAFETY comment
Add (or extend) a safe abstraction for it in the subsystem's Rust code, and use that from the driver
Rewrite the C function in Rust inside the driver so no FFI is needed
Use `extern "C"` to declare the function by hand in the driver
explain: The general-information doc says leaf modules such as drivers should not use the C bindings directly; subsystems provide as-safe-as-possible abstractions. Declaring the symbol yourself is the same forbidden shortcut with less checking. Duplicating the C logic would create a second implementation to maintain.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
question: A callback receives `t: &Task`. You want a work item to log that task's pid a few seconds later. What do you store in the work item?
options: `ARef::from(t)`: it takes a reference with get_task_struct and drops it with put_task_struct when the work item is dropped
`t` itself, as a `&'static Task` obtained with `core::mem::transmute`
`Arc::new(t)`, which shares the task between the callback and the work item
A bitwise copy of the C `task_struct`
explain: Only the ARef owns an increment of the task's real count. The transmuted reference compiles but nothing keeps the task alive: a use-after-free waiting to happen. `Arc::new(t)` would allocate a new object holding a borrowed `&Task` whose lifetime still ends with the callback, so it does not extend anything. Copying a task_struct copies pointers it does not own.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
question: Code under review creates `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` once to read and validate a header, then creates a second `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` to read the whole request and use it. What is the problem?
options: It is a double fetch: user memory can change between the two readers, so the validated header is not the one being used
Nothing: `copy_from_user` re-validates the data on every call
It cannot compile, because a `UserSlice` can only be created once per address
The second reader starts where the first one stopped, so it misses the header
explain: Each reader consumes its own UserSlice and advances independently, so the second one starts at the beginning again. `copy_from_user` checks the *address range*, not the contents. The uaccess.rs docs show exactly this pattern labelled as a TOCTOU bug and advise one UserSlice per user memory block.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
X, because the global DSQ is consumed before ops.dispatch() is ever called
Y, because custom DSQs have priority over built-in ones
Neither until ops.dispatch() chooses between them
explain: The pick order is fixed: local DSQ, then global DSQ, then ops.dispatch(). X is taken from the global DSQ without consulting the BPF scheduler. Y only moves if ops.dispatch() later calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(7).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
question: Your enqueue inserts a task into custom DSQ 3 while CPU 5 is idle. Nothing kicks CPU 5, and the other CPUs never read DSQ 3 in their dispatch. What can happen?
options: CPU 5 polls custom DSQs and notices within one tick
The kernel moves custom DSQ tasks to the global DSQ after one slice
The task waits while CPU 5 stays idle, until some CPU happens to dispatch from DSQ 3 or the watchdog fires
The verifier rejects enqueue callbacks that do not kick a CPU
explain: An idle CPU runs the scheduling path only when it is woken: by select_cpu choosing it, by a kick, or by new work in its local DSQ. Custom DSQs are only read by dispatch callbacks, so an unread queue plus no kick leaves the task stranded.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
question: After loading your scheduler, SCX_EV_SELECT_CPU_FALLBACK in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events climbs steadily. What does it point to?
options: The scheduler keeps entering bypass mode
Tasks are being inserted without a slice
Your select_cpu returns CPUs the tasks cannot use, and the core silently picks another one
The watchdog is about to declare a stall
explain: The kernel docs define it as ops.select_cpu() returning a CPU unusable by the task, after which the core picks a fallback. Look for a missing check against p->cpus_ptr, the task's allowed cpumask.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Revocation at scale: CircleCI and rotating every secret at once
question: A breach report says secrets were stolen on 22 December, and you finish rotating on 9 January. Which window do you search your own logs for misuse of those secrets?
options: Only 4 January, the disclosure date
From the earliest possible compromise (16 December here) until your rotation finished on 9 January
From 22 December onward
Only after 9 January
explain: Investigate the whole period a stolen copy could have worked: from the earliest date the vendor could not rule out until your rotation completed. CircleCI's own advice was 16 December through the date you rotated.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
